props.title: Monsieur Verdoux

sections.content: Monsieur Verdoux (1947) marks Charlie Chaplin's boldest departure from his Little Tramp persona, crafting a pitch-black comedy about a suave serial killer who marries and murders wealthy widows. The film's timing was explosive - released just after WWII, its cynical take on capitalism and morality shocked audiences who still wanted Chaplin's lighter fare. Like Dr. Strangelove (1964) would later do with nuclear war, Verdoux uses dark comedy to skewer society's acceptance of mass killing in war while condemning individual murder.

sections.content: The film's influence on dark comedies about murder can't be overstated. Kind Hearts and Coronets (1949) followed closely with its similarly genteel murderer, while later films like American Psycho (2000) and A Simple Favor (2018) continue the tradition of mixing sophistication with homicide. Chaplin's performance as Verdoux established a template for the charming sociopath that would influence Anthony Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs (1991) and Michael Caine in Sleuth (1972).

What makes Verdoux particularly daring is its direct challenge to post-war morality. When Verdoux compares his murders to the mass killings of war and business, the film becomes a savage critique of capitalism itself. This political edge got Chaplin labeled as a communist sympathizer and contributed to his eventual exile from America. Similar themes would later emerge in films like Network (1976) and The Wolf of Wall Street (2013), where the line between business and criminality blurs. SUBHEAD: From Slapstick to Satire

movies.slug: Alec Guinness leads a gang of criminals undone by a sweet old lady in this pitch-perfect dark comedy

sections.content: The transformation of Chaplin's screen persona from The Little Tramp to Verdoux represents one of cinema's most dramatic artistic evolutions. While films like The Great Dictator (1940) showed Chaplin's growing political awareness, Verdoux abandoned physical comedy almost entirely for verbal wit and subtle menace. This shift parallels later comedic actors who moved into darker territory, like Bill Murray in Lost in Translation (2003) or Robin Williams in One Hour Photo (2002).
